3.text: be established with certainty. Some people of poor standing and of violent

4.text: temper often purposely seek to drive their few reindeer into the herd of some

5.text: rich reindeer-breeder. This is more apt to be the case in summer, when the

6.text: herds are pasturing too near each other. On the Arctic coast, in the Kolyma

7.text: country, when a rich man comes too near the shore in summer, he always

8.text: incurs the risk of such unwished-for intermingling of herds. The strip of the

9.text: shore close to the water, which is cool and rich in vegetation, is occupied

10.text: by the poor people; and their small herds often mix together, so that this

11.text: strip of land is a ground of constant strife and quarrel. Still, among them-

12.text: selves the poor are able to separate without much loss. When, however, a

13.text: rich man arrives with his herd, his position is more difficult. The other party

14.text: then has an opportunity to slaughter his reindeer, to mark the fawns with the

15.text: thief’s own ear-mark, and to change the marks of grown animals.

16.text: The owner of a large herd does not know all his animals, and some of

17.text: the less conspicuous may even be abstracted without his being able to detect

18.text: it. Therefore the owner of a large herd always keeps at a distance from the

19.text: other camps, and, besides, is on the alert against the approach of another

20.text: herd. The separation of herds, even when performed without any fraud, is a

21.text: long and tiresome affair; so that the herdsmen are quite ready to use physical

22.text: force to prevent encroachers from coming too near. I often witnessed such

23.text: mingling of herds, which ended in quarrel and squabbling. The Reindeer

24.text: Tungus, when they live with the Chukchee, have a strong inclination to mix

25.text: their herds, because they are poor and move with their reindeer and tents

26.text: even in summer, while the Chukchee stay in the same place during that

27.text: season. When separation is again accomplished, the Chukchee complain that

28.text: several of their animals are missing. The Tungus, on the other hand, talk

29.text: about the loss of some well-broken animal which was of especial value. Since

30.text: the Tungus reindeer, though less numerous, are of superior quality and of

31.text: higher price than the Chukchee animals, both contending parties have cause

33.text: It goes without saying that a man cannot join a camp if he is not

34.text: allowed to do so by its inhabitants. Even in the very temporary camps at

35.text: trading-places or in those established at large reindeer-races, where many of

36.text: the participants come with a travelling-tent and family, no one can pitch his

37.text: tent near the others without previous permission. After this is given and the

38.text: reindeer are unharnessed, the herd immediately joins the common herd, because

39.text: the general rule is, one camp, one herd. Even here separation of the reindeer

40.text: leads afterwards to quarrels. The reindeer brought to such gatherings are of

41.text: greater value, well-broken, strong coursers, or fat animals intended for slaughter;

42.text: and the loss of even one counts.
